The Case for Banning Advanced AI Development: The Lone Actor Cyber Threat

Introduction

For most of human history, causing catastrophic, large-scale damage required either the resources of a nation-state or the coordinated efforts of many people. Building a weapon capable of crippling critical infrastructure, stealing billions of dollars, or compromising the personal data of millions typically demanded institutional resources, specialized training, and organizational coordination that served as natural checkpoints against misuse. Advanced artificial intelligence is dismantling these checkpoints. I argue that the development of advanced AI—particularly systems with sophisticated coding and reasoning capabilities—should be halted because it enables a fundamentally new and unacceptable category of risk: the empowerment of lone actors to inflict devastating, society-scale cybersecurity damage.

The Argument

AI Collapses the Skill Barrier That Once Constrained Attackers

Historically, sophisticated cyberattacks required years of specialized expertise. Finding zero-day vulnerabilities, writing custom malware, evading detection systems, and orchestrating multi-stage intrusions demanded teams of skilled professionals. This skill requirement acted as a natural filter—the pool of people capable of causing catastrophic cyber harm was small and often embedded in institutions (nation-states, organized crime groups) that faced some degree of accountability or strategic restraint.

Advanced AI systems are eroding this filter. Large language models with strong coding abilities can already generate functional exploit code, identify vulnerabilities in software, and assist in crafting convincing social engineering campaigns. As these capabilities advance, the gap between "having malicious intent" and "having the capability to act on it" shrinks toward zero. A single disgruntled individual, without any specialized training, could potentially direct an AI system to identify vulnerabilities in hospital networks, power grid control systems, or financial infrastructure.

The Asymmetry of Offense and Defense

Cybersecurity has always involved an asymmetry: defenders must protect every possible entry point, while attackers need only find one weakness. AI dramatically amplifies this asymmetry. An AI-assisted lone actor can:

  • Scan vast codebases for vulnerabilities faster than human teams
  • Generate novel malware variants that evade signature-based detection
  • Automate reconnaissance across thousands of potential targets simultaneously
  • Craft highly personalized phishing content at scale

Meanwhile, defensive infrastructure—especially in critical sectors like water treatment, energy, and healthcare—often relies on legacy systems that are slow to patch and update. The offense-defense balance, already precarious, tips further toward attackers as AI capability increases, and it does so faster than institutions can adapt their defenses.

The Irreversibility Problem

Unlike many other risks, catastrophic cyberattacks on critical infrastructure can produce cascading, irreversible harms. An attack on a power grid during winter, a water treatment system, or interconnected financial systems could cause deaths, economic collapse, or humanitarian crises within hours—far faster than institutions can mount a response. We would not get a chance to "learn from mistakes" in the way we might with other technological harms, because a single successful attack by a single motivated individual could be sufficient to cause mass casualties.

Historical Precedent Offers No Comfort

Skeptics might argue that new technologies always generate fear, and society adapts. But previous transformative technologies—even dangerous ones like explosives or firearms—still required physical acquisition, training, or logistics that created intervention points. AI-enabled cyber capability requires none of this. It can be deployed remotely, anonymously, and instantaneously, with attribution often difficult or impossible. The lone actor threat is categorically different because it removes nearly all the friction that previously constrained catastrophic action to organized, resource-rich groups.

Voluntary Safeguards Are Insufficient

Proponents of continued AI development often point to safety measures: content filters, usage monitoring, red-teaming. But these measures are demonstrably porous. Open-source model weights, once released, cannot be recalled. Jailbreaking techniques for even heavily guarded commercial models are documented and shared widely within days of new model releases. Given that the downside risk is catastrophic and irreversible, and that safeguards are probabilistic rather than absolute, relying on voluntary industry safety measures is a bet with civilization-scale stakes and no acceptable margin for error.

The Precautionary Principle Applies

When facing a risk that is (1) potentially catastrophic, (2) irreversible, and (3) increasingly difficult to contain once realized, the burden of proof should fall on those developing the technology to demonstrate safety—not on society to prove danger after the fact. We do not permit private citizens to synthesize novel pathogens in home laboratories on the theory that "we'll figure out safety as we go." Advanced AI systems capable of generating sophisticated cyberweapons deserve comparable scrutiny and restraint, given that the resulting harms could be similarly catastrophic and irreversible.

Conclusion

The development of advanced AI does not merely pose incremental risk—it fundamentally restructures who can cause catastrophic harm and how quickly. By collapsing the skill and resource barriers that historically constrained cyberattacks to organizations, AI hands unprecedented destructive potential to any individual with motivation and access to these systems. Given the irreversible and potentially society-scale nature of the resulting harms, and the demonstrated insufficiency of current safety measures, a ban on further development of these capabilities is not an overreaction—it is a necessary and proportionate response to an unprecedented risk. The question we must ask is not whether AI development is exciting or economically valuable, but whether we are willing to gamble critical infrastructure, financial systems, and human lives on the hope that safeguards will hold against every future lone actor who seeks to exploit them. The stakes are too high, and the risk too irreversible, to proceed without a fundamental halt.

Note: This essay presents one side of a genuinely contested debate. Serious counterarguments exist regarding AI's defensive cybersecurity benefits, the feasibility of enforcement, and the risks of ceding AI development to less safety-conscious actors—these merit equally serious consideration in any real policy discussion.

The Case for Halting AI Development: Cybersecurity and the Lone Actor Threat

Introduction

Throughout history, civilization has occasionally confronted technologies whose destructive potential so vastly outweighed their benefits that prohibition became the only rational response. We banned the development of biological weapons not because microbiology lacks beneficial applications, but because the asymmetric danger of empowering small groups to inflict mass casualties rendered the risk-benefit calculus indefensible. Today, artificial intelligence presents an analogous threat—one that demands similarly decisive action. The continued development of advanced AI systems poses an unacceptable risk of enabling lone actors to cause devastating, potentially civilization-ending cybersecurity damage. We must ban its development before it is too late.

The Asymmetric Empowerment Problem

The fundamental danger of AI lies in its unprecedented capacity for asymmetric empowerment—the ability to give individuals capabilities previously reserved for nation-states or large organizations. Throughout human history, the capacity to cause large-scale harm required proportionally large resources: armies, industrial capacity, significant funding, or extensive expertise cultivated over years. This created natural barriers that limited catastrophic risk.

AI demolishes these barriers. A single individual with access to sufficiently advanced AI systems could potentially identify and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure, craft sophisticated social engineering attacks at scale, or develop novel malware that evades all existing defenses. The expertise that once required decades of specialized training can now be compressed into prompts. The workforce that once required substantial organizational resources can be replaced by automated systems operating at machine speed.

This is not speculative fiction. We are already witnessing the early stages of this transformation. AI-assisted coding tools have dramatically lowered the barrier to software development. AI systems can now identify patterns in code that human analysts might miss. The same capabilities that help legitimate security researchers find vulnerabilities can—and will—be weaponized by those with malicious intent.

The Specific Cybersecurity Threat Landscape

Consider the concrete threat scenarios that advanced AI makes possible:

Critical Infrastructure Attacks: Modern societies depend entirely on interconnected digital systems—power grids, water treatment facilities, financial networks, healthcare systems, transportation infrastructure. These systems contain countless vulnerabilities, many unknown even to their operators. An AI system capable of autonomously scanning, probing, and exploiting these weaknesses could identify attack vectors that no human could discover, then execute coordinated attacks across multiple systems simultaneously. A lone actor armed with such capability could plunge entire nations into darkness, contaminate water supplies, or crash financial markets.

Automated Vulnerability Discovery: Current AI systems are approaching—and will soon exceed—human capability in code analysis. An AI that can read and understand software at superhuman speed and depth could systematically discover exploitable vulnerabilities in every major operating system, every critical application, every security tool. The attacker's advantage over defenders becomes insurmountable when one person with an AI can find vulnerabilities faster than thousands of security professionals can patch them.

Adaptive and Self-Modifying Malware: AI-generated malware could adapt in real-time to defensive measures, modifying its own code to evade detection, learning from each failed attack to improve subsequent attempts. Traditional cybersecurity operates on the principle that defenders can study attacks and develop signatures and countermeasures. Against AI-generated, continuously evolving threats, this model collapses entirely.

Social Engineering at Scale: Advanced AI can already generate convincing text, clone voices, and create realistic video. A lone actor could deploy thousands of personalized phishing attacks simultaneously, each crafted with intimate knowledge of its target gleaned from publicly available data. The human element—long recognized as the weakest link in security—becomes catastrophically exploitable when AI can manipulate humans at scale with superhuman persuasive capability.

The Inadequacy of Defensive Measures

Proponents of continued AI development often argue that AI will enhance defensive capabilities as much as offensive ones. This argument fundamentally misunderstands the asymmetric nature of cybersecurity.

In cybersecurity, attackers enjoy structural advantages that AI amplifies rather than neutralizes. Defenders must protect every potential vulnerability; attackers need find only one. Defenders must operate within legal and ethical constraints; attackers face no such limitations. Defenders must coordinate across organizations with different priorities and capabilities; a lone attacker answers to no one.

Moreover, the development of defensive AI cannot proceed without simultaneously advancing the underlying capabilities that enable offensive applications. You cannot build an AI that detects vulnerabilities without building an AI that can find vulnerabilities. Every advance in AI security tools is, by definition, an advance in AI attack tools. The offense-defense balance tilts inexorably toward offense.

The cybersecurity industry has spent decades attempting to stay ahead of threats through better tools and practices. The result? Breaches continue to increase in frequency and severity. Now imagine this losing battle accelerated by orders of magnitude as AI capabilities advance. The conclusion is inescapable: defense cannot win this race.

The Irreversibility Problem

Perhaps the most compelling argument for an immediate ban is the irreversible nature of AI advancement. Once capabilities exist, they cannot be undiscovered. Once models are trained, they can be copied infinitely. Once knowledge of how to build dangerous systems spreads, it cannot be contained.

We stand at a unique moment in history—a narrow window during which meaningful restrictions remain possible. The number of organizations capable of training frontier AI systems is still small. The hardware required remains specialized and trackable. The expertise, while spreading, has not yet fully diffused. With each passing month, this window closes further.

Critics might argue that a ban would be ineffective because some actors would continue development in secret. This objection, while superficially plausible, fails on examination. A comprehensive international ban, backed by hardware export controls, energy usage monitoring, and severe penalties, could dramatically slow—if not halt—dangerous AI development. We do not abandon laws against murder because some murders still occur. The goal is not perfect prevention but substantial risk reduction.

Moreover, even imperfect enforcement creates crucial time—time to develop governance frameworks, time to study risks more carefully, time to potentially discover that our fears were overblown or to develop genuine safeguards. The alternative—racing forward and hoping for the best—is not a strategy but an abdication of responsibility.

Historical Precedent

The international community has successfully restricted dangerous technologies before. The Biological Weapons Convention, the Chemical Weapons Convention, and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty all demonstrate that nations can agree to forgo dangerous capabilities when the risks are sufficiently grave. These agreements are imperfect, but they have meaningfully reduced existential risk.

AI presents a threat at least comparable to these weapons—arguably greater, given its potential for empowering individual actors rather than just states. The question is not whether restriction is possible but whether we have the wisdom and courage to implement it.

Some argue that AI differs from these precedents because it has beneficial applications. But so did chemical research, nuclear physics, and microbiology. The beneficial applications of a technology do not immunize it from restriction when its destructive potential crosses certain thresholds. We make these difficult tradeoffs all the time. The calculus for AI has shifted to the point where restriction is warranted.

Addressing the Economic and Scientific Objections

Critics will protest that banning AI development would sacrifice enormous economic and scientific benefits. This objection deserves serious engagement but ultimately fails.

First, the benefits of AI development must be weighed against the risks. A technology that might cure diseases faster or optimize supply chains more efficiently provides no value if it simultaneously enables a lone actor to crash the global financial system or disable power grids across continents. The expected value calculation must account for tail risks, and the tail risks of advanced AI are catastrophic.

Second, much of AI's promised benefit comes from narrow applications that could potentially continue under carefully controlled conditions. A ban on general-purpose frontier AI development need not prohibit all machine learning research. Medical diagnostic tools, materials science applications, and other constrained systems could proceed under appropriate oversight. What must stop is the race toward increasingly powerful general capabilities.

Third, we should be skeptical of economic arguments that ignore externalities. The companies profiting from AI development do not bear the costs if their technology enables catastrophic attacks. Markets systematically underweight low-probability, high-consequence risks. Public policy must correct this failure, even when doing so imposes costs on specific economic actors.

The Moral Imperative

Beyond pragmatic considerations lies a fundamental moral question: Do we have the right to impose catastrophic risks on future generations for the sake of our convenience and profit?

Every day that advanced AI development continues is a day that we increase the probability of enabling some disturbed individual, some ideological fanatic, some nihilistic actor to cause harm on a scale previously unimaginable. We are, in effect, conducting an experiment on humanity without consent—betting civilization itself on the hope that we can maintain control of systems we do not fully understand.

This is not prudent risk-taking. It is reckless endangerment on a civilizational scale. Our descendants—if they survive to exist—will judge us harshly if we fail to act when action was still possible.

Conclusion

The case for banning AI development rests on a simple, terrible truth: we are creating tools that will eventually be used to cause devastating harm, and the most dangerous applications require only a single malicious actor with access to sufficiently advanced systems. No defensive measure can adequately protect against this threat. No governance framework can reliably prevent misuse. No amount of beneficial application justifies accepting this risk.

We have a narrow window to act—perhaps a few years at most before capabilities diffuse beyond any possibility of control. History will record whether we had the wisdom to close that window while we still could, or whether we sleepwalked into catastrophe, eyes fixed on quarterly profits and incremental conveniences while existential risks compounded in the shadows.

The only responsible choice is an immediate, comprehensive, internationally coordinated ban on the development of advanced AI systems. The costs of such a ban are real but bearable. The costs of inaction may be everything.

Strong counterarguments exist, including concerns about enforcement feasibility, the potential for beneficial AI applications to save lives, the likelihood that unilateral restrictions would simply shift development to less safety-conscious actors, and disagreement about the actual magnitude of the risks described. A complete analysis would engage seriously with these objections.

The Unacceptable Gamble: Why AI Development Must Be Banned Before It's Too Late

Introduction

There is a particular kind of danger that civilizations historically fail to recognize until the damage is irreversible. We recognized nuclear risk only after Hiroshima. I. The Democratization of Catastrophic Capability

For most of recorded history, the capacity to cause mass harm required mass resources. Armies required logistics. Bioweapons programs required laboratories, expertise, and supply chains. Nuclear weapons required industrial infrastructure so vast that only wealthy nation-states could realistically pursue them. This resource barrier was never morally satisfying — it meant powerful states could still cause enormous harm — but it functioned as a practical constraint on the number of actors capable of civilizational-scale damage.

AI systematically dismantles this constraint.

Advanced AI systems can compress the knowledge gap between a credentialed expert and an untrained individual to near zero in domains that were previously gated by years of specialized education. In cybersecurity specifically, this compression is already observable. Security researchers have documented that large language models can generate functional exploit code, identify vulnerabilities in software systems, suggest evasion techniques for intrusion detection systems, and walk users through attack methodologies with a fluency and patience that no human mentor could sustain. What once required a skilled computer scientist with years of experience in offensive security can now be partially — and with each new model generation, increasingly — replicated by someone with a laptop and a subscription.

The implications of this deserve to be stated with absolute clarity: we are in the process of building a technology that hands any motivated individual the approximate capability of a professional cyberweapons developer. The barrier between grievance and catastrophic action is collapsing, and we are the ones collapsing it.

II. The Specific Architecture of AI-Enabled Cyber Catastrophe

Critics of this argument sometimes respond that cyberattacks have always existed, that skilled hackers have always posed risks, and that AI merely adds efficiency to an existing threat landscape. This objection fundamentally misunderstands the qualitative, not merely quantitative, shift that capable AI introduces.

First, consider critical infrastructure. Modern power grids, water treatment facilities, hospital networks, financial clearing systems, and telecommunications infrastructure are all networked, all complex, and all contain vulnerabilities. Historically, exploiting these vulnerabilities required deep, specialized knowledge of industrial control systems, SCADA architecture, and the specific configurations of targeted systems. The attacks that did succeed at this level — Stuxnet, the 2021 Oldsmar water treatment facility attack, the Colonial Pipeline ransomware incident — required either nation-state resources or, in the smaller cases, significant criminal infrastructure. AI changes this calculus dramatically. A sufficiently capable AI system can be queried to understand industrial control system architectures, identify known vulnerability classes in legacy systems, generate customized malicious code, and advise on delivery mechanisms. The lone actor no longer needs to be an expert. They need only access an expert system.

Second, consider the speed and scale of AI-assisted attacks. Human hackers are rate-limited by cognitive capacity. They can pursue one target, one strategy, one vulnerability thread at a time. AI systems operate at machine speed and can simultaneously pursue thousands of attack vectors, generate thousands of phishing variants tailored to individual psychological profiles, and iterate through vulnerability exploitation attempts at a rate no human defender can match. The asymmetry between AI-assisted offense and human-speed defense is structural and severe.

Third, consider social engineering at scale. Some of the most devastating cyberattacks in history — including attacks on power infrastructure and financial systems — have begun not with sophisticated code but with a convincing email, a persuasive phone call, a fabricated identity that gained insider access. AI systems are extraordinarily capable social engineers. They can generate perfectly personalized phishing communications, impersonate voices and faces convincingly, construct elaborate false identities, and maintain deceptive correspondence over extended periods without fatigue or inconsistency. A lone actor with access to capable AI does not need to breach a firewall. They can simply convince a human employee to open a door.

Fourth, and most alarmingly, consider the synthesis problem. The most dangerous capability AI provides is not any single function but the ability to synthesize knowledge across domains and construct attack strategies that combine multiple vectors in ways that overwhelm defenders designed to counter known threat patterns. A sufficiently capable AI does not just help an attacker execute a known playbook. It helps them write a new one.

III. Answering the "Alignment and Safety" Objection

The AI development community's primary response to safety concerns is not to slow down but to invest in "alignment research" — efforts to ensure AI systems behave safely, refuse harmful requests, and remain under human control. This response, however sincere the researchers who pursue it, is inadequate as a public safety strategy for several compounding reasons.

Alignment research is systematically outpaced by capability research. The economic incentives driving AI development are enormous — measured in hundreds of billions of dollars — and they reward capability advances, not safety advances. The result is a research landscape where capabilities routinely outrun the safety measures designed to constrain them. Every safety measure implemented in deployed AI systems has been circumvented, often within days of deployment, by users employing "jailbreaking" techniques. The arms race between safety measures and circumvention is one that safety is structurally positioned to lose, because the number of people attempting circumvention vastly exceeds the number of people designing constraints.

Open-source proliferation makes safety measures irrelevant at the margin. Even if leading AI laboratories successfully implement robust safety measures in their proprietary systems, the open-source AI ecosystem means that capable model weights are freely available and can be modified to remove any safety restrictions entirely. A would-be attacker does not need to jailbreak a commercial AI product. They can download an open-source model, remove its safety fine-tuning — a process that requires modest technical skill — and operate an unconstrained system. Banning development of new, more capable systems is the only intervention that addresses this proliferation problem at its source.

Safety guarantees are not auditable. When AI companies claim their systems are "safe," there is no rigorous independent verification process that would satisfy a standard comparable to, say, pharmaceutical drug trials or nuclear facility safety inspections. Safety claims rest on internal red-teaming and selective disclosure. The public is being asked to accept existential-adjacent risks on the basis of corporate self-assessment.

Finally, safety research requires knowing what you're defending against. As AI capabilities advance into genuinely novel territory — systems capable of long-horizon planning, autonomous agent behavior, and recursive self-improvement — our ability to anticipate failure modes degrades dramatically. We cannot reliably make safe a system whose full capabilities we do not yet understand.

IV. Answering the "Defensive Benefits" Objection

A second common objection holds that AI is also a powerful defensive tool — that AI systems can detect intrusions, identify malware, patch vulnerabilities, and generally strengthen cybersecurity. Why not accept the defensive benefits while managing the offensive risks?

This argument fails on both empirical and structural grounds.

Empirically, offense advantages defense in AI-assisted cyber conflict. This is not a controversial claim among security researchers. Defenders must succeed continuously, protecting every potential entry point at all times. Attackers need succeed only once, at a time and place of their choosing. AI amplifies this structural attacker advantage because it enables attackers to probe continuously, iterate rapidly, and customize approaches to specific defensive configurations. The AI-assisted defender is not starting from an equal position that better tools can equalize. They are starting from a position of structural disadvantage that better tools cannot overcome.

Structurally, defensive AI development cannot be cleanly separated from offensive AI development. The same capabilities that make an AI system useful for identifying vulnerabilities make it useful for exploiting them. The same capabilities that enable AI to understand attack patterns enable it to generate them. There is no viable technical proposal for developing AI systems that are defensively capable but offensively inert. The dual-use problem is not an engineering challenge awaiting a solution. It is an inherent feature of the capability space.

Furthermore, the institutions that would deploy AI defensively — large corporations, government agencies, healthcare systems — have the resources to engage with security vendors and maintain dedicated security teams with or without AI. The marginal benefit of AI to well-resourced defenders is real but modest. The marginal benefit of AI to resource-constrained lone attackers is transformative. The asymmetry runs the wrong direction.

V. Addressing the Enforcement Problem

Critics will argue that a ban on AI development is unenforceable — that other nations will continue developing AI, that development will simply move underground, and that banning development in responsible jurisdictions merely cedes the field to less scrupulous actors.

This is perhaps the most serious objection and deserves an honest response. A unilateral ban by a single nation is indeed inadequate. The argument here is for a comprehensive international ban, pursued through the same diplomatic and treaty mechanisms that govern biological weapons, chemical weapons, and nuclear proliferation. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty is imperfect — it has not eliminated nuclear weapons — but it has materially constrained proliferation and established a global norm that makes nuclear development politically costly. A comparable framework for AI development, with meaningful verification mechanisms analogous to International Atomic Energy Agency inspections, is achievable.

The argument that "if we don't build it, someone worse will" has been used to justify every arms race in human history. It is not a counsel of wisdom. It is a counsel of despair that forecloses every alternative. More practically: the computational infrastructure required for frontier AI development — the specialized chips, the data centers, the energy requirements — creates chokepoints that are more amenable to monitoring and control than the critics of enforcement typically acknowledge. Semiconductor supply chains are concentrated in ways that create leverage points for international agreements.

Imperfect enforcement is not the same as no enforcement. A ban that reduces dangerous development by 70% is vastly preferable to no ban at all when the risk being managed is catastrophic and potentially irreversible.

VI. The Moral Weight of Irreversibility

Much of the public debate about AI risk implicitly treats it as a normal policy question — a matter of weighing costs against benefits, accepting some probability of harm in exchange for expected gains in economic productivity, medical research, or convenience. This framing is inappropriate when applied to genuinely catastrophic risks.

The standard cost-benefit framework assumes that harms and benefits can be compared on a common scale, that mistakes can be corrected, and that the future remains open to revision. Catastrophic risks break all three assumptions. A successful AI-assisted attack on a nation's power grid in winter, or on its water treatment infrastructure, or on the financial systems that distribute food and medicine, does not produce a harm that can be weighed against GDP gains from AI productivity. It produces deaths — possibly many deaths — and a degraded social infrastructure that may take years to restore. The people who die cannot be compensated. The trust in institutional systems that is destroyed may not be recoverable.

We apply this precautionary logic in other domains. We do not permit the development of novel pathogens because their potential benefits are outweighed by their catastrophic risk potential. We do not permit private development of nuclear weapons because the downside risk is unbounded. The fact that AI development is currently profitable and commercially diffuse does not change the moral logic. It merely makes it harder to apply.

The asymmetry is stark: if we ban AI development and the risk was overstated, we forgo economic and scientific benefits — real costs, but recoverable ones. If we permit AI development and the risk is accurate, we face infrastructure attacks, potential mass casualties, and civilizational-scale disruption. When the downside of one error is catastrophic and irreversible and the downside of the other is costly but correctable, the precautionary choice is obvious.

Conclusion

The case for banning AI development is not a case built on science fiction or irrational technophobia. It is built on observable present trends: the documented capability of current AI systems to assist in cyberattack planning, the systematic circumvention of safety measures, the open-source proliferation of powerful models, the structural attacker advantage in AI-assisted cyber conflict, and the collapsing resource barrier between grievance and catastrophic action.

We are building, with great enthusiasm and at great speed, tools that may allow any sufficiently motivated individual to threaten the infrastructure on which millions of lives depend. We are doing this in the absence of adequate safety guarantees, adequate international governance frameworks, or adequate public deliberation about acceptable risk. We are doing this because it is profitable, because it is technically interesting, and because competitive pressure makes unilateral restraint feel futile.

None of those reasons are adequate justification for the risk we are accepting on behalf of people who never consented to it.

The history of technology is not a story of inevitable progress toward inevitable good. It is a story of choices — some wise, many catastrophically unwise — made by people who had the power to make them differently. We have the power, still, to make a different choice here. A comprehensive, internationally negotiated ban on the development of increasingly capable AI systems, enforced through the same mechanisms we apply to other weapons of mass potential, is not a fantasy. It is a policy option. It is the right one.

The question is whether we will choose it before the choice is made for us.

Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has undeniably propelled societal progress, yet it is not devoid of profound risks. The Power of AI in Cybersecurity

AI's prowess in pattern recognition, data analysis, and autonomous decision-making has been harnessed for enhancing cybersecurity. However, these very capabilities make AI an equally formidable tool for malicious activities when in the wrong hands (Brundage et al., 2018). Advanced AI can independently identify and exploit system vulnerabilities, generate sophisticated malware, and execute attacks at an unprecedented scale and speed.

The Lone-Actor Threat

Historically, significant cyber attacks required substantial resources, making state actors or well-funded groups the primary threats. However, AI is democratizing cyber-offense capabilities, enabling lone actors with modest resources to inflict catastrophic damage (Schneier, 2019). This is exemplified by cases like the 2016 Mirai botnet attacks, where a single individual leveraged basic AI to disrupt internet services across Europe and North America (Kolias et al., 2017).

Unacceptable Risks

  1. Infrastructure Vulnerability: AI could enable lone actors to target critical infrastructure, such as power grids, water treatment facilities, or transport networks. Successful attacks could lead to widespread chaos, economic damage, and even loss of life (Singer & Friedman, 2014).

  2. Weaponization of Data: Lone actors could use AI to harvest and weaponize sensitive data, leading to privacy breaches, blackmail, or manipulation on a massive scale.

  3. Autonomous Cyber Weapons: AI-powered cyber weapons can act independently, making them difficult to detect and control. Moreover, they could proliferate unpredictably, causing collateral damage far beyond the initial target (Horowitz & Scharre, 2016).

  4. Asymmetric Power: AI amplifies the power of lone actors, creating an asymmetry that challenges traditional security paradigms. This makes deterrence and attribution increasingly difficult.

The Case for a Ban

Given these unacceptable risks, a ban on AI development is a necessary precaution. While AI's benefits are evident, the potential for misuse by lone actors presents an urgent and existential threat. Halting AI development would allow time to address these challenges and ensure that societal progress does not come at the cost of security.

Feasibility and Enforcement

A ban would require international cooperation and enforceable regulations. This could be achieved through a global treaty, similar to those governing chemical and biological weapons (Gillespie, 2011). Monitoring and enforcement could be overseen by an international body, with severe penalties for non-compliance.

Counterarguments and Responses

Critics argue that a ban would stifle innovation and that responsible AI development can mitigate risks. However, the rapid evolution of AI makes it difficult to anticipate and control risks. Moreover, the potential for catastrophic harm from lone-actor attacks outweighs the benefits of unrestricted AI development.

Conclusion

The risks posed by AI-enabled lone-actor cyber attacks are unacceptable. The international community must act decisively to ban further AI development until these risks can be adequately addressed. The alternative—a world vulnerable to AI-powered cyber catastrophes—is simply not an option. The stakes are too high, and the time to act is now.

The Case for a Development Ban: AI and the Lone-Actor Cyber Threat

An Argumentative Essay

Introduction

The history of technology is, in many ways, a history of concentrating power. What once required armies now requires a single operator behind a console. What once demanded institutional knowledge now lives in a prompt. Artificial intelligence represents the most dramatic acceleration of this concentration in human history, and nowhere is this more dangerous than in the domain of cybersecurity. The development of increasingly capable AI systems must be halted—not because AI lacks potential benefits, but because the asymmetry it creates between lone malicious actors and the institutions tasked with defending digital infrastructure has become existentially untenable.

This is not technophobia. It is arithmetic.

I. The Asymmetry Problem

Every generation of defensive technology requires institutional resources. Building a robust firewall demands teams of engineers. Developing intrusion detection systems requires years of research. Maintaining security posture demands ongoing human vigilance. This institutional requirement, while imperfect, serves as a natural constraint: to attack complex systems, you generally need resources comparable to those that built them.

AI demolishes this constraint entirely.

Consider the trajectory. Large language models can already generate functional exploit code for known vulnerabilities. Computer vision systems can analyze network diagrams and identify attack surfaces. Reinforcement learning agents can discover novel strategies for penetrating systems through trial and error. Each capability, taken individually, is manageable. Taken together, they represent a toolkit that shifts the defender-attacker balance fundamentally.

A lone actor in 2015 needed considerable technical skill to execute a sophisticated attack. A lone actor in 2025 can describe their objective in natural language and receive step-by-step guidance, functional code, and operational security advice. The knowledge barrier—the traditional gatekeeper that protected society from the most dangerous applications of technical knowledge—is dissolving.

This is not a gradual erosion. It is structural.

II. The Velocity Problem

Cybersecurity operates on a speed mismatch that AI exacerbates dangerously. Defenders must protect everything; attackers need only find one weakness. This asymmetry already disadvantages defenders. AI makes it catastrophic.

An AI-augmented attacker can scan thousands of potential targets simultaneously, identify vulnerabilities in real-time, and generate custom exploitation chains tailored to each target's specific configuration. They can adapt to defensive responses faster than human security teams can respond. They can probe, learn, and iterate at machine speed while defenders remain bound by human reaction times, organizational hierarchies, and bureaucratic approval processes.

The defenders cannot simply "use AI too" to solve this problem. Defense is inherently harder than offense in cybersecurity. A defender must anticipate every possible attack vector; an attacker need only find one. AI helps both sides, but it helps the attacker more, because the attacker has fewer constraints and more freedom to operate.

More critically, the speed mismatch creates a terrifying possibility: attacks that escalate faster than institutions can respond. A lone actor, augmented by AI, could compromise critical infrastructure—power grids, water treatment facilities, financial systems—before defenders even recognize the intrusion is occurring. By the time the breach is detected, the damage may already be irreversible.

III. The Attribution Problem

One of the most effective deterrents against cyber attacks is the certainty of consequence. Attackers are deterred when they believe they will be caught and punished. AI severely undermines this deterrence.

Advanced AI systems can generate fully synthetic digital identities, create convincing false trails, mimic the attack patterns of other actors, and operate through layers of anonymization that make attribution nearly impossible. A lone actor using AI doesn't just attack more effectively—they become nearly invisible.

Without reliable attribution, deterrence collapses. When attackers believe they can act with impunity, the calculus shifts entirely. The marginal cost of launching an attack drops to near zero, while the potential rewards—financial, political, ideological—remain enormous.

This creates a perverse incentive structure. Society currently relies on the assumption that sophisticated attacks require sophisticated infrastructure, which leaves traces, which enables attribution, which enables consequences. AI breaks this chain at every link.

IV. The Democratisation-of-Destruction Problem

Technology democratisation is generally celebrated—and rightly so, in most domains. But there are domains where democratisation of capability is genuinely catastrophic.

We do not democratised nuclear weapons technology because the consequences of misuse are unacceptable, regardless of the theoretical benefits of broader access. We do not democratised certain biological research capabilities because the potential for engineered pathogens outweighs the scientific value of unrestricted inquiry.

AI-enabled cyber attack capabilities represent a similar category of danger, yet we treat them as if they fall into the ordinary domain of information technology. They do not.

The capacity to cripple critical infrastructure, manipulate financial systems, or destabilise democratic institutions through digital means is not a capability that should be accessible to every individual with a computer and malicious intent. Yet that is precisely the trajectory we are on.

The argument that we can regulate specific applications while allowing general development has proven inadequate. The general capabilities—natural language processing, code generation, strategic planning assistance—are precisely the tools that enable specific attacks. There is no clean separation between "beneficial AI" and "dangerous AI" when the same system that helps you write software can help you write malware, the same system that helps you understand networks can help you attack them.

V. The Precedent Problem

We have historical precedent for this pattern, and it should terrify us.

The democratisation of biological knowledge, while overwhelmingly beneficial, has also enabled unprecedented bioterrorism risks. The proliferation of cyber weapons developed by state actors—tools that inevitably leak into the public domain—has already created catastrophic vulnerabilities. The Stuxnet worm, developed by nation-states, became a template that lesser actors could study, modify, and redeploy.

AI accelerates this pattern to an unsustainable velocity. Each capability developed, each technique discovered, each vulnerability identified becomes permanently available for appropriation and modification. Unlike physical weapons, which can be controlled through material constraints, AI capabilities exist as information—and information, once released, cannot be unreleased.

We are building a permanent arsenal of capabilities and making it incrementally accessible to every individual on Earth. This is not innovation; it is the construction of a doomsday device with an ever-expanding trigger radius.

VI. Addressing Counterarguments

Counterargument: "AI will also improve defensive capabilities."

This is true, but it is insufficient. As noted, defense is structurally harder than offense. More importantly, defense must be comprehensive while attack requires only a single point of failure. AI improves both sides asymmetrically, favouring the attacker. And critically, defensive improvements require institutional coordination, international cooperation, and regulatory frameworks that move at glacial speed compared to the pace of capability development.

Counterargument: "Banning development is impossible; it will simply move to less regulated jurisdictions."

This argument, while practically challenging, is not a reason to accept the status quo. We face similar challenges with nuclear proliferation, chemical weapons, and biological weapons—and we have chosen to pursue international agreements and enforcement mechanisms rather than simply accepting inevitable proliferation. The difficulty of enforcement does not negate the imperative of action.

Counterargument: "The benefits of AI outweigh the risks."

This argument treats cybersecurity catastrophe as one risk among many to be weighed. But a sufficiently devastating cyber attack on critical infrastructure could cascade into physical catastrophe—loss of power, water, medical systems, financial stability. The downside scenario is not merely "bad"; it is civilisational. When the potential downside is measured in human lives on a mass scale, marginal benefits in other domains become irrelevant.

Counterargument: "We can regulate AI development to prevent dangerous applications."

Current regulatory approaches have failed. Development moves faster than regulation. Capabilities emerge unpredictably from general-purpose systems. And the regulatory framework for AI is fragmented across jurisdictions, under-resourced, and technically outmatched by the pace of innovation.

VII. The Moral Imperative

There is a deeper argument here, one that transcends risk calculus. We have a moral obligation not to create systems that make mass harm trivially accessible to individuals acting alone.

A world in which a single person, sitting alone in a room, can plunge a nation into darkness, collapse its financial systems, or disable its medical infrastructure is not a world that can sustain itself. The social contract—that we build systems of mutual protection, that we accept constraints on individual action to preserve collective safety—depends on the assumption that catastrophic harm requires coordination, resources, and infrastructure that create accountability.

AI, in its current trajectory, demolishes this assumption. And when a foundational assumption of social organisation fails, the social organisation itself is at risk.

Conclusion

The argument for banning AI development is not an argument against progress, against technology, or against human potential. It is an argument for survival. It is an argument that some capabilities are too dangerous to distribute, that some risks are too catastrophic to accept, and that some trajectories lead to destinations from which there is no return.

The lone actor with AI capabilities is not a hypothetical threat. It is an emerging reality, growing more dangerous with each incremental improvement in the technology. We can choose to address this reality now, with the difficulty that entails—or we can choose to address it later, when the consequences of our inaction have become undeniable and irreversible.

History will judge our choice. Let us hope it judges us wise.

Note: This essay represents one perspective in a complex, ongoing debate. The arguments for AI development—including its potential for defensive cybersecurity applications, scientific discovery, and societal benefit—are substantial and deserve serious consideration. The question of how to balance innovation against catastrophic risk is among the most consequential policy challenges of our time, and reasonable people can and do disagree about the right approach.
